energy-flow-s2.title: Biomass at each level in a grassland

plot.label: Bar chart of dry biomass at four trophic levels in a grassland: grasses 1,500, grazers 120, small predators 11, large predators 1.5 g/m², invented data

items.q: Producers in a meadow store 20,000 kcal/m²/yr. Using the 10% rule, about how much energy reaches the secondary consumers?

why.correct: Two steps up (producers → primary → secondary): $20{,}000 \times 0.10 \times 0.10 = 200$ kcal/m²/yr.

mistakes.why: That is the primary consumers (one step). Secondary consumers are two steps up: × 0.10 twice.
You applied the 10% rule three times. Producers to secondary consumers is two steps.

items.q: Primary consumers in a forest store 3,000 kcal/m²/yr. Write the setup for the energy reaching tertiary consumers by the 10% rule, then give the answer.

why.correct: Primary → secondary → tertiary is two steps: $3{,}000 \times 0.10 \times 0.10 = 30$ kcal/m²/yr.

mistakes.why: That is three steps. From primary to tertiary consumers is two steps.
That reaches secondary consumers. Tertiary consumers are one more step up.
You applied the rule three times. Primary to tertiary is two steps.
That is the secondary consumers. Go one more step.

items.q: Why is only about 10% of the energy at one trophic level passed to the next?
options: Most is lost as heat in respiration.
Energy is destroyed each time an animal eats.
Predators eat just 10% of the prey they catch.
Producers keep 90% of the sunlight for later.

why.correct: Organisms use most of the energy they take in for respiration, movement and body heat, and some food is never eaten or is lost in waste. Energy is not destroyed; it leaves as heat.
options: Right: respiration, heat, uneaten parts and waste.
Energy is never destroyed; it changes form (first law of thermodynamics).
The 10% is about energy passed on, not the share of prey caught.
Producers use their energy in their own respiration; they do not save it for consumers.

items.q: Which law explains why some energy becomes unusable heat at every transfer between trophic levels?
options: The second law of thermodynamics
The first law of thermodynamics
The 10% rule of photosynthesis in plants
The law of conservation of mass

why.correct: The second law says every energy transfer turns some energy into heat that is less useful, so no transfer is 100% efficient.
options: Right: transfers lose some energy as heat.
The first law says energy is conserved, not that it is lost as heat.
The 10% rule describes the result; it is not a law of physics.
Mass conservation is about matter, not energy quality.

items.q: Why does an ecosystem usually have no more than four or five trophic levels?
options: Too little energy is left at the top.
Predators at the top run short of water.
Producers make too little oxygen for more.
Decomposers eat the animals at the top level.

why.correct: With about 10% passing up each step, after four or five steps there is too little energy to support a population of a larger predator.
options: Right: energy runs out going up.
Water is not what limits chain length.
Oxygen is plentiful; energy is the limit.
Decomposers feed on dead matter from all levels.

items.q: Why can a given area of farmland feed more people if they eat grain directly than if the grain is fed to cattle and people eat the beef?
options: Eating grain skips a trophic step.
Beef has more calories per kilogram than grain does.
Cattle make new energy from the grass they eat.
Grain plants are secondary consumers in the field.

why.correct: Each step up loses most of the energy. People eating grain are primary consumers; eating beef from grain-fed cattle adds a step.
options: Right: one fewer step means more energy reaches people.
Even so, cattle lose most of the grain’s energy to respiration and heat.
Cattle cannot make energy; they get it from plants.
Grain comes from producers.

items.q: A hawk population needs about 50 kcal/m²/yr of food energy. The hawks are tertiary consumers. Using the 10% rule, how much energy must producers store?

why.correct: Tertiary consumers are three steps above producers: $\frac{50}{0.10 \times 0.10 \times 0.10} = 50{,}000$ kcal/m²/yr.

mistakes.why: You multiplied by 0.10 three times. Going down the chain, divide by 0.10 at each step.
That is two steps. Producers to tertiary consumers is three steps.

items.q: In an energy pyramid, what does the width of each level show?
options: The energy at that level
The number of species at that level
The body size of each organism there
The average age of the organisms there

why.correct: An energy pyramid shows energy per area per time at each level; it always narrows going up.
options: Right: energy at each level.
Species counts are not what an energy pyramid shows.
Body size is not shown.
Age is not shown.

items.q: What percent of the producers’ energy is passed to the primary consumers?

mistakes.why: 0.11 is the fraction. Multiply by 100 for a percent.
You divided the lower level by the higher. The energy passed on (880) goes on top.

items.q: What is the transfer efficiency from small fish to bass, as a percent?

mistakes.why: That is the fraction. Multiply by 100 for a percent.

items.q: Which statement do the data support?
options: Each transfer is close to 10%.
Each level holds about half the energy of the level below.
Energy increases at the higher trophic levels.
The bass get about 10% of the producers’ energy.
Right: each step is close to 10%.
Each level holds about a tenth, not half.
Energy falls at each level.
Bass get 7/8,000, about 0.09% of the producers’ energy.

items.q: What percent of the producers’ energy reaches the bass?

why.correct: $\frac{7}{8{,}000} \times 100 = 0.0875\%$, less than a tenth of a percent.

mistakes.why: 8.75% is the last step only (small fish to bass). Compare the bass with the producers: 7 / 8,000 × 100.
That is the fraction. Multiply by 100 for a percent.

items.q: Which pattern does the biomass chart show?
options: It falls sharply at each level.
It rises at each higher trophic level.
Each level has about the same biomass.
Grazers have more biomass than grasses.

why.correct: 1,500 → 120 → 11 → 1.5 g/m²: roughly a tenth or less at each step.
options: Right: a sharp drop each step.
The bars get shorter going up.
The bars differ greatly.
Grasses (1,500) far exceed grazers (120).

items.q: What best explains why the grazers’ biomass is so much smaller than the grasses’?
options: Grazers lose most energy as heat.
Grazers eat just a tiny share of the grass.
Grasses photosynthesize faster at night.
Grazers are eaten by the grasses they graze.

why.correct: Less energy reaches each level, so less tissue can be built and supported there.
options: Right: energy lost as heat limits the biomass above.
Even if grazers ate much more, most energy would still be lost as heat.
Photosynthesis needs light.
Grasses do not eat animals.

items.q: The grassland covers 50 m² in a study plot. What is the total dry biomass of the grazers in the plot, in grams?

mistakes.why: You divided. Multiply grams per m² by the area in m².
That uses the grasses (1,500 g/m²). The question asks about the grazers (120 g/m²).
